name: Agrarianism
summary: Agrarianism holds that rural life centred on independent family farms is the best basis for a free and virtuous society. It favours widespread small property, decentralised local self-government and republican politics, and distrusts industry, finance, cities and dependent wage labour. It spans left and right, from Jeffersonian and Southern Agrarian traditionalism to agrarian socialism and Nordic centrist farmers' parties.
scope: Agrarianism as Britannica (F. Eugene Heath) defines it: the view that stresses the primacy of family farming, widespread property ownership and political decentralisation, anchored in the two texts it names, Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia (1785) and the Southern Agrarians' I'll Take My Stand (1930). It also names John Taylor, Crevecoeur, Bailey, Borsodi, Chesterton, Belloc and Wendell Berry, but those texts were not read. Physiocracy, agrarian socialism, Maoism and agrarian parties are not the basis.

keyFigures.role: Author of the Jeffersonian ideal of independent farmer-citizens as the basis of a republic.
keyFigures.quote: For Taylor, as for Jefferson, it was the free farmer whose independence was crucial for citizenship.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The Statement of Principles says an agrarian society is not one with no use for industries, professions, scholars and artists, only one where agriculture is the leading vocation.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The Statement of Principles condemns the ideal of "industrial progress, or an incessant extension of industrialization", whose labour-saving devices evict laborers and cause "increasing disadjustment and instability".

alienated-labor.rationale: The Statement of Principles says that under the industrial regime labour becomes mercenary and servile, is "hard, its tempo is fierce", and is practised solely for its rewards instead of as a happy function of life.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Britannica says the agrarian shares with certain environmentalists a strong concern about the factory farming of animals.

automate-paid-work.rationale: The Statement of Principles denies that saving labour is a pure gain, holding that whether a labour-saving machine benefits depends on how far it is advisable to save the labour.

bound-labor.rationale: The agrarian ideal is the independent farmer who owns his land and so is truly free, the opposite of a farmer legally tied to an estate.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The Statement of Principles says the capitalization of the applied sciences has "enslaved our human energies", and Britannica says agrarianism challenges the notion of progressive industrialization.

collective-farming.rationale: Britannica says agrarianism stresses the primacy of family farming, which collective farms replacing individually operated farms would end.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Britannica says the agrarian life discourages the ambitious pursuit of material goods, and the Statement of Principles says industrial consumption leaves people in "satiety and aimlessness" and condemns advertising for coercing consumers.

decide-locally.rationale: Britannica names "political decentralization" as one of the three things agrarianism stresses above all, with a stable local community as its setting.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Jefferson wrote that those who depend on "the casualties and caprice of customers" are made subservient, and the SAGE entry says true freedom belongs to the independent farmer.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The Statement of Principles says a community groaning under industrialism, "an evil dispensation", must find the way to throw it off, and holds that it brutalises labour, religion, the arts and manners.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The Statement of Principles rejects the capitalised industrial economy as an evil and calls the Communist menace a menace too, and Britannica sets agrarianism against both corporate capitalism and egalitarian democratic doctrines.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Britannica says agrarians criticise the corporation as an artificial creature of the state that has secured ever more legal privileges and subsidies, and John Taylor decried using the law to favour factional and commercial interests.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Twelve Southerners were vocal in their intense hatred of communism and fascism, the two one-party systems of their day.

person-over-state.rationale: The Statement of Principles objects to sacrificing private dignity and happiness to an abstract social ideal and says men's responsibility is for their own welfare and their neighbours', not for a "fabulous creature called society".

positive-liberty.rationale: The SAGE Encyclopedia of Politics says agrarianism holds that true freedom belongs to the independent farmer who owns his or her own land, so freedom rests on a material base.

religion-illusion.rationale: The Statement of Principles treats religion as submission to the general intention of a nature fairly inscrutable and the sense of our role as creatures, a truth that industrial life destroys, not an illusion.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Jefferson wrote that the earth is given as a common stock to labour on and that, if we allow it to be appropriated, other employment must be furnished to those excluded, or the right to labour the earth returns to the unemployed.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The Statement of Principles holds that the culture of the soil is the best and most sensitive of vocations and should have the economic preference, which leaves no room for foraging as better.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Jefferson wrote that those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God, that city mobs are sores on the body politic, and that the share of non-farmers in a state measures its corruption.

simple-living.rationale: Britannica says the agrarian life would discourage the ambitious pursuit of material goods and enable a nonacquisitive enjoyment of leisure, friendship and art.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Jefferson proposed exempting everyone below a certain point from taxation and taxing higher portions of property "in geometrical progression as they rise", to lessen inequality.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The Statement of Principles says the remedies of industrialism look only to bigger and better machines and more industrialism, and calls this a homeopathic cure for evils the machines themselves bring.

total-state.rationale: Agrarianism stresses decentralisation, and the Statement of Principles denounces an economic super-organisation that would become the government and says the responsibility of men is for their own and their neighbours' welfare, not an abstract society.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: EBSCO reports that the authors of I'll Take My Stand were vocal in their intense hatred of both communism and fascism.

traditional-family.rationale: Britannica says agrarianism emphasises family, rooted family and locale, and the Statement of Principles lists family life among the amenities that industrialism damages.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Jefferson tied the concentration of property in a few hands to mass wretchedness and urged devices for subdividing it, and held that dependence breeds subservience and prepares tools for ambition.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Britannica defines agrarianism by "widespread property ownership", and Jefferson urged legislators to devise every means to subdivide property so that few are without a little land, calling small landholders the most precious part of a state.
